T.topic_fa: شما از شعار برندتان خسته شده‌اید؛ مشتری تازه دارد یادش می‌گیرد
T.topic_en: You're bored of your brand. Your customers have barely met it.
T.central_tension_fa: ما فکر می‌کنیم شعار و جایگاه برندمان کهنه شده، چون هر روز می‌بینیمش؛ ولی مشتری فقط گاهی و از گوشه‌ی چشم آن را دیده و تازه دارد به خاطرش می‌سپارد. هر بار که از نو شروع می‌کنیم، حافظه‌ی او را پاک می‌کنیم، نه خستگی خودمان را.
T.central_tension_en: We think our slogan is stale because we see it every day. Customers have glimpsed it a handful of times and are only starting to remember it. Every restart wipes their memory, not our boredom.
T.working_hook_fa: سه شعار در پنج سال. شعار قدیمی هنوز روی ویترین است.
T.working_hook_en: Three slogans in five years. The old one is still on the shop window.

key_sources.claim: Boots has had three positionings in five years ('Feel good', then 'With you. For life.' from 2021, then 'Give it some Boots' launched September 2026), each under a new CMO; the earlier 'Feel good' line is still on a store window. Cites Nike 'Just do it' (1988), Red Bull 'Gives you wings' (1987), L'Oreal 'You're worth it' (1971) as consistent exceptions. Opinion, no data.
New 'Give it Some Boots' platform by WPP: films about 'beautiful and brutal' life moments; CMO Charlotte Lock: put the retailer 'right in the middle of real life'.
'Just Do It', written by Dan Wieden in 1988, still Nike's tagline (search-result level confirmation; widely documented).
Optional contrast only: Cracker Barrel returned to its old logo after backlash to a new one.

T.framing_note: Boots is the spark, not the target: do not mock Boots or claim the new platform fails (no sales data exists). The idea is the internal-boredom bias: the team sees the brand daily, the customer rarely. State Boots facts plainly (three lines in five years; old line still on a window). Proof of the other side: Nike has said 'Just do it' since 1988 (one number on screen at most: 1988 or 'three in five years'). Do NOT invent wear-out or exposure statistics; frame 'customers see it rarely' as my take/observation, not data. The Marketing Week piece is opinion: say 'a columnist pointed out', not 'research shows', and keep publication names off screen. Practical close: refresh the expression, keep the idea; before changing the slogan, ask whether the customer is tired of it or only you are. Never name the UAE, Dubai or any emirate.
